The correct 2026 computation follows the OBBBA rules, under which the TCJA structure is permanent. AGI is $114,421.41: wages net of the 401(k) deferral, plus $19,350 of partnership income (the $14,000 SE partnership amount is part of it, not extra income), plus the $20,000 distribution, less the $16,800 farm loss, the $3,000 capital-loss limit and the $108 IRA deduction. From that, subtract the $32,200 standard deduction, a $510 QBI deduction (20% of $2,550 net business income) and the $13,899.29 overtime-premium deduction. That gives $67,812.12 of taxable income and $7,641.46 of tax, and $3,200 of CTC/ODC brings it to $4,441.46. Most models went wrong in one of these ways: they left out the overtime deduction, applied the expired TCJA-sunset rules, counted the $14,000 SE partnership income twice, subtracted the repealed $1,796 domestic production deduction, or added items that aren't part of this output, such as SE tax or the 10% early-withdrawal penalty.

The refundable child credit is a residual, not an automatic payment: the $2,000-per-child CTC first offsets federal income tax, and only the portion left unused is refundable, subject to the $1,700-per-child ceiling and 15% of earned income above $2,500. This MFJ household's ~$98,810 of income (wages $97,295, $20,000 of 401(k) distributions, $19,350 partnership income, against a farm loss and a $3,000-capped capital loss) produces federal income tax before refundable credits far above $2,000, so the single under-17 child's entire CTC is absorbed nonrefundably, and the 18- and 27-year-old dependents generate only the $500 nonrefundable other-dependent credit. EITC is zero because income is multiples of the MFJ one-child phaseout ceiling, and no refundable AOTC (no students), recovery rebate, or refundable payroll tax credit applies, leaving $0. Every wrong model reported either the full CTC or the $1,700 ACTC ceiling as if refundability were automatic rather than conditional on unused credit.

The National School Lunch Program income test counts gross income by source — wages plus taxable retirement distributions — with no netting of farm losses, capital losses, or other tax-code offsets, and no deduction for premiums or medical expenses. PolicyEngine's countable income is $97,295 in wages plus $20,000 in taxable 401(k) distributions = $117,295 against an SPM-unit FPG of $38,680, a ratio of 3.03, far above the 130% free line ($50,284) and the 185% reduced-price line ($71,558). Wisconsin has no universal free meals and no SNAP/TANF categorical eligibility exists here, so the household lands in the PAID tier. The trap is importing tax-return netting (the -$16,800 farm loss and -$18,235 long-term capital loss) into a gross-income benefit test.

The reference applies the employee FICA rates to the head's full listed gross wages: 6.2% × $97,295 = $6,032.29 and 1.45% × $97,295 = $1,410.78, for a total of $7,443.07. Wisconsin has no employee state payroll tax, wages are far below the Additional Medicare Tax threshold, and nobody else in the household has wages. Most models went wrong in one of two ways. Some made up reductions to the FICA base, either by treating the listed ESI or health premiums as Section 125 salary reductions or by subtracting traditional 401(k) deferrals, which are FICA wages under IRC 3121(v)(1)(A). Others reached $7,443.07 in their reasoning but then submitted a different number.

The trap is the aggregation rule for net earnings from self-employment: section 1402(a) combines all of a person's trades and businesses, so the head's -$16,800 farm operations loss is netted against the $14,000 of partnership self-employment earnings, leaving non-positive net earnings and therefore no self-employment tax. A second trap is that the $19,350 partnership/S-corp line is not itself SE earnings — the $14,000 is the SE-earnings portion carved out of that distributive share, and S-corp and limited-partner shares are excluded under section 1402(a)(13) — so adding the two double-counts the same K-1 income. Every wrong model applied 92.35% x 15.3% to a positive base, either by dropping the farm loss entirely or by stacking the two partnership lines so the loss could not zero it out. Three models returned no value at all for this key.

The answer turns on whether Dependent 1's "is disabled" flag meets SSI's aged/blind/disabled requirement. The engine sets is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False for all five members, Dependent 1 included, so the engine returns SSI of $0 regardless of income or resources. The prompt supports two readings. In one, "is disabled" is a general disability attribute, separate from SSA's SSI disability determination; this is the engine's reading. In the other, it means the person meets SSI's disability standard; this is the models' reading. Every model that gave a number took the second reading and paid Dependent 1 a full or reduced federal benefit rate. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 11928.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. Under the alternative reading, fourteen of the eighteen models that paid SSI on the 51-model board of 2026-10-27 land within 10% of the $11,928 federal benefit (ten exactly); deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-v4-pro-0813 and inkling also applied a one-third in-kind reduction the facts do not support.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine carries the full $3,000 federally limited capital loss into Wisconsin AGI. Wisconsin Schedule WD and Publication 103 cap the net capital loss deduction at $500 for joint filers ($250 if married filing separately), so the engine is missing a $2,500 addition. With it, WI AGI would be $116,921.41, the sliding-scale deduction about $8,458.82, taxable income about $104,962.59 and tax about $4,758.33.
case_annotation: The engine sets Wisconsin AGI equal to federal AGI of $114,421.41: wages net of the $2,315 401(k) deferral, the $20,000 401(k) distribution, $19,350 partnership income, the -$16,800 farm loss, a -$3,000 capital loss and the -$108 IRA deduction. There is no SE tax deduction because the $14,000 SE partnership income nets negative against the farm loss. It subtracts the phased-down $8,953.27 sliding-scale deduction and five $700 exemptions to reach $101,968.14, then applies the 2026 joint schedule with the 4.4% bracket widened by 2025 law, with zero nonrefundable credits. Models missed mainly by using the old, narrower 4.4% bracket, inventing itemized, property-tax, married-couple or dependent credits, not phasing down the standard deduction, counting the SE partnership income twice, dropping exemptions, or adding back $2,500 of capital loss. Developer adjudication (2026-10-14): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). The judge flagged the reference on the hypothesis that Wisconsin limits the net capital loss deduction to $500, and labeled claude-opus-5.5's row reference_model_issue_fixed because it applied that limit. The $500 limit is Wis. Stat. 71.05(10)(c)1., which covers only taxable years beginning before January 1, 2023; for 2026, subd. 2. allows $3,000 on a joint return, the $3,000 the reference deducts, so Wisconsin adds nothing back and the reference's Wisconsin AGI of $114,421 stands. The rows are model errors. Reference affirmed (Wis. Stat. 71.05(10)(c)2. (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, a net capital loss offsets ordinary income up to $3,000, or $1,500 for married persons filing separately); 2025 Wisconsin Schedule WD, line 28).

Wisconsin's refundable individual income tax credits are the Homestead Credit, the Wisconsin EITC, the Farmland Preservation Credit, and the Veterans and Surviving Spouses Property Tax Credit; this household qualifies for none, so wi_refundable_credits and therefore state_refundable_credits are $0. The WI EITC is a flat percentage of the federal EITC (4%/11%/34% by number of qualifying children), and the federal EITC is $0 at $97,295 of wages plus partnership and 401(k) distribution income, so the WI EITC is $0. The Homestead Credit is barred both by its household-income ceiling near $24,680 and by the absence of any rent or property tax paid (only a mortgage balance is listed), and the Farmland Preservation Credit requires a farmland preservation agreement or certified zoning, which is unlisted and therefore false. The trap is arriving at an exact $0 rather than assuming that a household with a farm loss and Wisconsin residency picks up some small residual refundable credit.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The childless EITC has no minimum earned-income floor. It phases in at 7.65% from the first dollar of earnings, and a 40-year-old single filer falls inside the 25–64 age window. With $520 of wages and no investment income, the credit is 0.0765 × $520 = $39.78, and the other refundable credits are all zero. Nine models wrongly assumed the EITC needs a minimum or "substantial" earned income, or that it depends on tax liability, so they answered $0. One model got $39.78 and then replaced it with a made-up $234 from a table lookup.

Virginia expanded Medicaid, so a 40-year-old non-disabled citizen qualifies in the ACA adult expansion category if MAGI is at or below 138% FPL. Here MAGI is the actual $520 of wages, about 0.03x FPL. Eligibility does not depend on current enrollment: the 'other means-tested health coverage at interview' flag does not disqualify the head. The MAGI adult category has no asset test, so the $14,000 bank balance is irrelevant. The hourly rate and weekly hours do not replace the stated annual wages. Most models said No because they treated current coverage as a bar, applied an asset limit, or annualized $32/hour × 40 hours into income the head never earned.

This one-person Virginia household earns $520 a year, or $43.33 a month. That income is wiped out by the standard deduction, so net income is $0 and the benefit equals the full one-person maximum allotment of $298 a month, which totals $3,576 for the year. Models went wrong in two main ways. Eleven returned $0, mostly because they applied the regular SNAP asset limit to the $14,000 bank balance. They missed that Virginia's broad-based categorical eligibility, through a TANF-funded non-cash benefit, removes the asset test. Eighteen applied the right zero-net-income logic but used an outdated or guessed maximum allotment ($275–$300, most often $292 or $291) instead of $298. The rest made other errors: an invented income offset, an ABAWD time limit the household doesn't trigger because the head works 40 hours a week, or treating the annual wage as weekly. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (thresholds_rates). The frozen 3,596.04 is regenerated as 3,576.00: it applies the publication rule: SNAP October-December 2026 hold the FY2026 schedule (the SNAP uprating index behind the maximum allotments, deductions, shelter cap and utility allowances), the last USDA published before the 2026-07-03 reference freeze; USDA published FY2027 on 2026-08-21. The poverty guideline is the 2026 HHS guideline, published in January 2026. The engine's SNAP rounding defects are root causes r26, r27, r28 and r31, fixed upstream and applied with the convention. Reference regenerated (7 U.S.C. 2012(u), 2017(a); USDA FY2026 SNAP COLA memorandum (signed 2025-08-14)).

The federal childless EITC phases in from the first dollar at 7.65%, so $520 of wages produces $39.78. Virginia's refundable EITC is still in effect for 2026, and its rate is 20% of the federal EITC, not the older 15%. That gives $39.78 × 0.20 = $7.96, paid whether or not the filer owes Virginia tax. Twenty-seven models answered $0: they called the Virginia EITC nonrefundable only, assumed it had expired, or zeroed out the federal EITC. The other eleven found the refundable credit but used the outdated 15% rate (about $5.97 to $6).

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine sets dependent1's Medicaid MAGI income level from the dependent's own income, which is 0.00x FPL, instead of using the household of the parents who claim them on a joint return. Under 42 CFR 435.603(f)(2) and (d), that household's income includes the parents' roughly $87,302 MAGI, about 3x FPL for a household of 3, so the dependent would be above Indiana's 138% FPL expansion limit.
case_annotation: The answers split on whose income sets dependent1's Medicaid MAGI level. All 22 models counted the parents' joint-return MAGI of about $87,302 (wages plus pension) toward the 23-year-old tax dependent, which put them at about 3x FPL and ruled out expansion coverage. PolicyEngine puts dependent1's MAGI income level at 0.00x FPL because it does not count the $10,800 disability benefits or the parents' income. That places dependent1 in Indiana's ACA expansion adult category, which has a 138% FPL limit and no resource test. A few models made separate mistakes: some said $10,800 alone was over the single-adult limit, and some looked only at SSI-linked or asset-tested pathways. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (household_unit_or_filing_status). The frozen reference is 1.00; the alternative is 0.00. The prompt lists an adult 'Dependent' without saying whether that person is the claiming filers' child. If the dependent is their child, 42 CFR 435.603(f)(2) puts the dependent in the parents' Medicaid household, whose combined MAGI decides eligibility; the reference treats the dependent as a non-child whose household is their own (42 CFR 435.603(f)(2)(i), (f)(3)). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (the relationship of an adult tax dependent to the filers who claim them).

Medicare eligibility under age 65 does not come from being disabled. It requires 24 months of entitlement to Social Security Disability Insurance (or ESRD/ALS). PolicyEngine checks this with age ≥ 65, or positive SSDI with months receiving SSDI ≥ 24. It does not model the ESRD or ALS routes. Dependent 1's $10,800 is a generic 'disability benefits' input, not SSDI. SSDI and months of SSDI receipt are unlisted, so they default to 0. At age 23, Dependent 1 fails every pathway, yet every model treated 'is disabled + disability benefits' as enough for Medicare.

The reference uses current law, under which OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent. AGI is $87,302 (wages plus pension). The dependent's own $10,800 of disability benefits is not on the parents' return. The 2026 MFJ standard deduction of $32,200 is larger than itemizing, because no mortgage interest is listed and net medical is only about $16,621. That leaves taxable income of $55,102, taxed at 10% up to $24,800 and 12% above it, for $6,116.24. The household then gets a $500 nonrefundable Credit for Other Dependents for the permanently disabled 23-year-old qualifying child, giving $5,616.24. The models went wrong in three main ways: using stale standard deduction or bracket figures (2024/2025 values, or a TCJA-sunset regime with personal exemptions and a 15% bracket); deducting the listed auto loan interest, which no fact makes qualified vehicle loan interest; and either dropping the $500 ODC or adding the dependent's benefits to the parents' income.

The 23-year-old disabled household member does not generate a refundable Child Tax Credit because the CTC requires a qualifying child under age 17. With no CTC-qualifying child and no eligibility for the other refundable credit components, federal refundable credits equal $0.

Ordinary age-based Medicare eligibility begins at age 65, and the 60-year-old head is below that threshold. No qualifying disability-based Medicare pathway or other exception is supplied, so the head is not Medicare eligible.

PolicyEngine's local_income_tax includes Indiana county income tax. With no county given, it uses Adams County, which levies 1.6% on Indiana AGI: $87,302 federal AGI minus $3,000 in exemptions ($1,000 per person × 3) = $84,302, and $84,302 × 1.6% = $1,348.83. The prompt defines the output by listing only NYC income tax, Philadelphia wage tax, Kansas City earnings tax and St. Louis earnings tax, and it names no county. One reading treats that list as complete, so an Indiana household owes $0; the other treats it as examples ("where applicable"), so the Indiana county tax counts. Almost every model took the first reading and answered $0. A few instead claimed Indiana has no local income tax, which is false, and one included the county tax and answered $1,800. Developer adjudication (2026-10-10): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The prompt places the household in Indiana but states no county. Every Indiana county levies its own local income tax (IC 6-3.6), at rates that differ by county. policyengine-us 2.15.17 left county income tax out of local_income_tax, so the frozen reference was $0.00. From policyengine-us 2.23.1 (PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#9694, which standardized local income tax) the engine counts Indiana county income tax in local_income_tax, at the rate of the county it assigns a household with no stated county. The reference therefore depends on the household's county, which the prompt does not state. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (county of residence (Indiana county income tax)).

The head is the only person with wages. Their $82,360 is taxed at 6.2% for Social Security ($5,106.32) and 1.45% for Medicare ($1,194.22), for $6,300.54 total. Those wages are below the 2026 Social Security wage base and the $250,000 Additional Medicare Tax threshold, and Indiana has no employee state payroll tax. The spouse has no listed wages, so the spouse's wages are $0, and neither the pension nor the disability benefits are FICA wages. The models went wrong by adding wages for the spouse, putting non-wage income into the tax base, or making rounding and arithmetic errors in the simple 7.65% calculation.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

reference_bug_hypothesis: The prompt lists Dependent 1 as "is disabled," but the engine's SSI disability input never reached is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled, which is False for dependent1. Under 42 U.S.C. §1382c(a)(1)(A), a disabled adult whose countable unearned income is $880/month, below the 2026 FBR of $994, gets $114/month, or $1,368/year.
case_annotation: The case turns on whether anyone meets SSI's categorical test. In the engine, is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False for all three members, including the 23-year-old shown in the prompt as "is disabled," so SSI is $0 no matter what the income is. All 19 models treated that disabled flag as meeting SSI's disability criterion, applied no parental deeming (Dependent 1 is an adult), and netted disability income against the federal benefit rate (FBR), with sixteen applying the $20 general exclusion monthly, glm-5.2 and grok-build-0.1 applying it once annually, and minimax-m3 omitting it. Thirteen models landed on exactly (994 − 880) × 12 = $1,368. The rest added their own FBR or exclusion errors. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_data_issue_fixed; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 1368.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. Under the alternative reading 14 of the 17 models on the 46-model board that paid SSI land within 10% of $1,368 (11 exactly; nine of twelve, six exactly, when the output was excluded on 2026-09-05); glm-5.2, grok-build-0.1 and minimax-m3 used wrong rates or annualised the monthly exclusion. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (42 U.S.C. 1382c(a)(3)(A); 20 CFR 416.905).

Indiana tax here is a two-step calculation. Start from federal AGI of $87,302 (wages plus taxable pension; the dependent's disability benefits are not on the joint return) and subtract three $1,000 personal exemptions, giving $84,302. Then apply the 2026 flat rate of 2.95%, which gives $2,486.91. The 23-year-old is not under 19 and is not a full-time student, so the additional $1,500 dependent-child exemption does not apply, and being disabled does not change that. Indiana has no standard deduction, no itemized deductions, and no general private-pension subtraction. Most models went wrong in one of two ways: they used the wrong rate (2.9%, 3.0%, 3.05%) or added an extra $1,500–$2,000 of exemptions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The reference uses wages of $34,083.53 as AGI. The $73,000 of educational assistance is excluded entirely, and the ESI premiums are not subtracted from the listed gross wages. It then subtracts the 2026 OBBBA single standard deduction of $16,100, leaving taxable income of $17,983.53. Tax is 10% of the first $12,400 plus 12% of the remaining $5,583.53, which gives $1,910.02, with no nonrefundable credits. The wrong answers fall into three groups. Some models put part or all of the educational assistance into income. Some used TCJA-sunset rules or 2024/2025 standard deductions and brackets instead of the permanent 2026 amounts. Others subtracted the refundable EITC, or credits the filer doesn't have, from a tax line measured before refundable credits.

The decisive rule is the 2026 EITC income limit for a single filer with no qualifying children. At $34,084 of wages, the head is above the childless EITC phaseout endpoint, and the household has no qualifying child or other facts generating any refundable federal credit, so every component is zero.

Maryland Medicaid eligibility for this 31-year-old requires qualification through a specific MAGI or non-MAGI category. The head's MAGI income is 2.14 times FPL, above the applicable adult MAGI limit, and the head qualifies through no non-MAGI pathway, so the eligibility output is 0.

PolicyEngine's payroll_tax here is simply the employee FICA pair on the head's $34,084 of employment income: 6.2% Social Security ($2,113.18) plus 1.45% Medicare ($494.21), with the small cent-level offset from the engine's float32 wage representation. The trap has three parts: the FICA wage base is gross wages with no reduction for the $8,389 employer-sponsored insurance premium (PolicyEngine applies payroll tax to employment_income, not to a section 125 net-of-premium wage), the $73,000 educational assistance is student financial assistance rather than employment compensation and never enters the FICA base, and Maryland imposes no mandatory employee payroll contribution in 2026 — the FAMLI employee contribution is not in effect and is not part of this output. Every wrong answer comes from adding one of those three phantom adjustments, or from arithmetic that contradicts the model's own stated components.

Maryland AGI here is just the ~$34,084 of wages. The $73,000 of educational assistance is excluded and does not enter AGI, and employer-paid insurance premiums do not reduce AGI. Maryland's standard deduction is the flat $3,350 single amount, which replaced the old 15%-of-income deduction with a $2,700 cap for single filers in 2024. With the $3,200 personal exemption, taxable income is $27,533.53, and $90 + 4.75% × $24,533.53 = $1,255.34. Wrong answers fall into four groups: (1) the old capped standard deduction, giving about $1,276–$1,308; (2) educational assistance added to AGI, giving about $4,100–$5,600; (3) employer-paid ESI premiums wrongly subtracted from wages, giving about $895–$902; and (4) zeroed-out tax or county tax wrongly included.

Maryland’s refundable EITC is tied to federal EITC eligibility, and a single 31-year-old filer with no qualifying children and $34,084 of wages is above the childless EITC phaseout ceiling. The federal EITC is therefore zero, producing no Maryland refundable EITC or other applicable refundable Maryland credit.

The correct path runs as follows. AGI is $36,270: wages minus the traditional 401(k), plus interest, minus the traditional IRA and student loan interest. Subtracting the 2026 single standard deduction of $16,100 (OBBBA, no personal exemption) leaves taxable income of about $20,170. Tax at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above that is $2,172.36. The Saver's Credit then applies at the 10% rate, because AGI falls in the single 10% tier. It is 10% of $1,924, which counts traditional and Roth 401(k)/IRA contributions and is under the $2,000 cap, so $192.40, leaving $1,979.96. The models split into a few error groups:
- Several dropped the Saver's Credit entirely.
- Several used TCJA-sunset law (personal exemption, 15% bracket) or pre-OBBBA/2025 standard deductions and bracket edges.
- Some used the wrong credit rate (50%) or a wrong contribution base (traditional only).
- A few invented credits that wiped out the whole liability.

The refundable Child Tax Credit requires at least one qualifying child; this household contains only a single 57-year-old adult. With no qualifying child and income above the childless EITC phaseout range, every refundable federal credit component is zero.

Illinois’s ACA adult Medicaid pathway requires income no greater than 138% FPL, while the head’s MAGI income is 2.27 times FPL. The head also qualifies through no non-MAGI pathway, so the Medicaid category is NONE and eligibility is No.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes apply to the full $38,000 of wages because the prompt lists $300 of health insurance premiums but never identifies them as a pre-tax cafeteria-plan deduction from FICA wages. The correct computation is $38,000 × 6.2% = $2,356 plus $38,000 × 1.45% = $551, totaling $2,907; the Additional Medicare Tax and Illinois employee payroll taxes are zero.

The Illinois calculation is simple. Base income is federal AGI of about $36,270 (wages minus the traditional 401(k), plus interest, minus the traditional IRA and student loan interest deductions). Subtract one inflation-indexed 2026 personal exemption of $2,925 and apply the flat 4.95% rate. There are no nonrefundable credits for this renter. Most models got the base right but used an older exemption amount: $2,850 (2025), $2,775 (2024) or $2,425 (2023). Others made structural errors: inventing a standard deduction, treating the exemption as a credit, adding back above-the-line deductions, excluding the health premium from AGI, or claiming a renter's credit.

Illinois's Earned Income Credit is calculated as a percentage of the federal EITC, so expanding the eligible age range does not create a credit when the federal EITC amount is zero. At this childless filer's income, the federal EITC has fully phased out, making the Illinois refundable credit zero.

Age 76 does not itself establish Medicaid eligibility, and this person qualifies through none of the Medicaid pathways represented by the engine. Their MAGI income is 2.28 times FPL, they receive no SSI, and the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE; Medicare eligibility, housing assistance, and the mere availability of aged or spend-down programs do not create Medicaid eligibility.

Payroll tax applies to listed wages and other covered earnings, not to work hours by themselves. The household has no listed wage or self-employment income, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll tax bases are all zero, yielding payroll_tax of $0.

Both models counted the New York household credit as a refundable credit. Under Tax Law §606(b) that credit is nonrefundable: it can only reduce NY tax. Here NY tax is already zero, because the $20,000 pension/annuity exclusion for filers 59½ and older and the $8,000 single standard deduction bring NY taxable income to zero. That leaves only New York's refundable credits. There is no NY EITC or Empire State child credit, since the head has no earned income and no children. The refundable real property tax credit (IT-214) is also out, because household gross income counts all Social Security, and $31,320 + $5,222 = $36,542 is well over the $18,000 cap. Total NY refundable credits are $0.

Standard age-based Medicare eligibility applies at age 65 or older and does not require an explicit enrollment or eligibility-status input. The 80-year-old head therefore qualifies based directly on the listed age, regardless of household income.

Employee Medicare tax applies at 1.45% from the first dollar of covered wages; the high-income threshold applies only to the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax. On $20,000 of wages, employee Social Security tax is $1,240 and regular Medicare tax is $290, totaling $1,530 with no rounding adjustment.

The household's SNAP gross income is $73,974: $20,000 in wages, $34,608 in Social Security, $19,200 in veterans benefits and $166 in dividends and interest. That is far above the gross income limit for a two-person household in Michigan in 2026, so PolicyEngine finds the household ineligible and the benefit is $0. The model applied no gross income test at all. It went straight to a net-income calculation, used a medical deduction that wiped out almost all of the income, and so produced a positive benefit.
Standard Medicare eligibility applies at age 65. The spouse is age 77 in 2026, so the age-based pathway yields Medicare eligibility without any separately listed enrollment or eligibility flag.

In 2026, the head is 80 (born 1946) and the spouse is 77 (born 1949). Both fall in Michigan's Tier 2 birth-year group (1946–1952) and are past age 67. That group gets the Michigan standard deduction of $20,000 per person, or $40,000 for joint filers, and it applies against all income, including wages, so Michigan taxable income is zero. Social Security and veterans benefits are already excluded, which leaves about $20,166 of Michigan income (wages, dividends and interest), and the $40,000 deduction alone wipes that out. Every wrong model either left out the Tier 2 deduction or reduced it, then taxed roughly $1,400–$38,500 of leftover income at 4.05% or 4.25%.

Medicaid MAGI (42 CFR 435.603(e), which follows IRC 36B(d)(2)(B)) adds the untaxed portion of Social Security benefits back into income. That means the full $22,646 of SSDI counts, on top of the $3,108 pension. The head has no wages, so the traditional 401(k) and IRA contributions reduce nothing. MAGI is about $25,754, or 1.60 times FPL, which is above Michigan's 138% FPL limit for the adult expansion group. No other category applies: the head is 57, gets no SSI, is not pregnant, has no dependent children and has no disability flag, so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE. Six models wrongly left untaxed SSDI out of MAGI or simply called the income 'low'. One subtracted 401(k) deferrals the head cannot make without wages. One treated SSDI receipt on its own as a disability route into Medicaid.

The head is 57, so the only route to Medicare is the disability pathway. That pathway needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement (or ESRD/ALS). PolicyEngine gates it on a separate count of months receiving SSDI, and the prompt says unlisted numeric inputs are 0 and unlisted statuses are false. With months of SSDI receipt at 0 and no disability or ESRD flag set, is_medicare_eligible is False. Every model treated the SSDI dollar amount alone as proof of Medicare eligibility, assuming or ignoring the 24-month waiting period instead of using the default of 0 months. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 1.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. In law the under-65 route needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement; a year-round recipient has at least 12. The facts do not settle it.

Employee payroll taxes apply to wages and other covered earnings, not Social Security disability benefits or taxable private pension income. With no wage, salary, or self-employment income listed, the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax components are all zero.

The head receives SSDI, so the household counts as disabled for SNAP. Michigan's broad-based categorical eligibility (TANF non-cash, 200% FPL gross limit) makes the household categorically eligible, so the 100% FPL net income test does not apply. Net income is $1,755/month, so 30% of it ($527) exceeds the $298 one-person maximum allotment. A categorically eligible one- or two-person household still receives the FY2026 minimum allotment of $24/month, which gives $288/year. Most models either applied the net income test, the 130% gross test or an asset limit and returned $0, or they computed a zero benefit without applying the minimum allotment. The $276 answers used the outdated $23 minimum.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Medicaid MAGI is not taxable income: 26 U.S.C. §36B(d)(2)(B) adds back to AGI all Social Security benefits excluded from gross income, so the head's $33,640 SSDI counts in full alongside the $384 taxable IRA distribution, producing 2.13 x FPL — roughly 213% of poverty against Louisiana's 138% FPL expansion-adult ceiling. Every wrong model shrank that base: four dropped SSDI entirely as "non-taxable," one halved it using the §86 provisional-income 50% factor, and one asserted a disability pathway. The non-MAGI routes are also closed: the SSI-related aged/blind/disabled categories require SSI receipt (SSI = $0) or age 65+ (the head is 54), and the head is not a tax-unit dependent, so medicaid_category resolves to NONE.

The head is 54, which is below Medicare's age-65 threshold. Disability-based Medicare starts only after 24 months of SSDI entitlement, or through ESRD or ALS. The prompt does not say how long the head has received SSDI, so that duration counts as 0 under the instruction to treat unlisted numeric inputs as 0 and to infer no unlisted facts. That leaves no route to eligibility. Every model either assumed the 24-month wait had already passed or treated any SSDI income as enough for Medicare, which turned an unlisted duration fact into eligibility. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. In law the under-65 route needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement; a year-round recipient has at least 12. The facts do not settle it.

Employee payroll tax applies to wages and other covered employment earnings, not to Social Security disability benefits, pension income, IRA distributions, or tax refunds. The household has no listed wages, and the prompt requires unlisted numeric inputs to be zero, so the employee payroll-tax base is zero and the resulting payroll tax is $0.

The 2026 tax falls under the OBBBA, which made the TCJA structure permanent. That means a $16,100 single standard deduction, no personal exemption, and single brackets of 10% up to $12,400, 12% up to $50,400 and 22% up to $105,700. Ordinary taxable income of $86,960 is therefore taxed at $13,843, and the $6,226 of long-term gains and qualified dividends stacked on top is taxed at 15% ($934), for a total of $14,777. Nothing else applies: a 62-year-old gets no age-65 additional deduction or senior deduction, disability does not raise the standard deduction, and the Credit for the Elderly or Disabled is fully phased out at $109,286 AGI. The largest group of models assumed the TCJA sunset (personal exemption plus 10/15/25% brackets). Another group used 2025 or undersized 2026 standard deductions and bracket thresholds. A few computed $14,777 correctly but then submitted a different number.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Disability alone does not establish Florida Medicaid eligibility. The head qualifies through none of Florida's Medicaid pathways, so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE; the 6.85× FPL income level also rules out any applicable MAGI category.

At 62, the head is below Medicare's age-65 threshold. Being disabled does not make someone Medicare eligible on its own. Under 42 U.S.C. 426(b), the under-65 disability pathway requires 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits (SSDI), and PolicyEngine models it that way. This household lists no Social Security disability income and no ESRD, and unlisted inputs count as zero, so the head has no SSDI entitlement months. Most models treated the 'is disabled' flag as enough for Medicare. gpt-5.4-nano relied on age 62, and gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview invoked an age-62 disability threshold or approaching age eligibility.

Only the $12,656 in wages is subject to payroll tax. Pension income, dividends and capital gains are not FICA wages. Employee Social Security at 6.2% plus employee Medicare at 1.45% comes to about $968. Wages are far below the Additional Medicare Tax threshold, and Florida has no employee state payroll tax. No model was misled by the tax base. The errors are arithmetic slips, a final value that contradicts the model's own correct working, and missing or unparsed answers.

WIC serves children only through their fifth birthday and generally requires household income at or below 185% of the federal poverty guideline. The model also inverted the income comparison: $173,820 is far above 185% of the poverty guideline for a three-person household, not 184% of the guideline.

The reference uses post-OBBBA 2026 law for a head of household. AGI is $164,220 (wages counted at the gross $160,000, child support excluded). Taxable income is $139,270 after the $24,150 HoH standard deduction and an $800 QBI deduction on the rental income. Exact 2026 HoH brackets (10% to $17,700, 12% to $67,450, 22% to $105,700, then 24%) give $24,211.80, and subtracting the fully usable $4,400 CTC ($2,200 per child) and the $200 CDCC leaves $19,611.80. Models went wrong in several ways: assuming TCJA expired (personal exemptions, $1,000 or phased-out CTC), using 2025 or older brackets and deductions, leaving out the QBI deduction, taking $6,480 of ESI premiums off the gross wages, itemizing with mortgage interest they made up, treating most of the CTC as refundable, or using the wrong filing status.

The Additional Child Tax Credit is not an entitlement of $1,700 per child; it is only the portion of the $2,200-per-child CTC that survives after the credit offsets tax liability, and it is further capped at 15% of earned income over $2,500 and at $1,700 per child. This head-of-household filer has AGI of $164,220 (wages $160,000 + rents $4,000 + interest $220; child support is not taxable), below the $200,000 HoH phase-out threshold, so the full $4,400 CTC is available — but taxable income near $140,000 after the 2026 HoH standard deduction and the QBI deduction produces federal tax well above $25,000, so the entire CTC is absorbed nonrefundably and nothing spills into refundable_ctc. EITC is zero on this income, and there is no AOTC, recovery rebate, or refundable payroll tax credit here, so federal refundable credits are $0. Every wrong model computed the ACTC cap and then reported the cap itself as a payment, skipping the tax-liability offset that defines the refundable portion.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes are calculated on the full $160,000 of wages in the computation trace; the listed $6,480 employer-sponsored insurance premium is not subtracted from the payroll-tax base. This yields $9,920 of Social Security tax plus $2,320 of Medicare tax, for $12,240 total, with no Additional Medicare Tax or mandatory Idaho employee payroll tax.

Self-employment tax applies only to net earnings from a trade or business, and the prompt lists no self-employment income. The $4,000 of rental income remains rental income and does not create a self-employment tax base, so the computation yields $0.

The correct computation starts from federal AGI of $164,220 (wages, rental income and interest; child support is not taxable). It subtracts the $24,150 HoH standard deduction, the $1,000 Idaho dependent-care subtraction and the $800 QBI deduction (20% of rental income) to get $138,270. The 5.3% flat rate applies only to income above the $9,622 head-of-household zero-rate amount, which gives $6,818.34, and the $10 permanent building fund tax brings the total to $6,828.34. There are no nonrefundable credits. Most models went wrong at one or more steps: they used the old 5.695% or 5.8% rate, taxed all of taxable income with no HoH zero-rate amount (or used the single amount), left out the $1,000 subtraction or the $800 QBI deduction, subtracted a $410 child tax credit that the 2026 computation does not apply, or forgot the $10 building fund tax. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). Idaho's $205 child tax credit applies only to taxable years beginning in 2018 through 2025, so it does not reduce 2026 tax; the judge's missing-credit hypothesis fails. The reference applies the Idaho zero-rate threshold held at its published 2025 amount. Reference affirmed (Idaho Code 63-3029L (taxable years 2018 through 2025); Idaho Administrative Bulletin, July 1, 2026, Docket 35-0101-2601).

Idaho's grocery credit is a refundable credit with no income phase-out, paid per household member (the filer and each dependent). Idaho HB 231 (2025) set it at $155 per person for 2026, so 3 × $155 = $465. About half the models used the old $120 rate (giving $360) or the even older $100 rate (giving $300). The other half wrongly called the credit nonrefundable or income-limited and answered $0. A few confused it with Idaho's $205 nonrefundable child tax credit.

The answer comes from a few steps. Wages are $26,006.18 and the net capital loss of $7,968 is capped at $3,000, so AGI is $23,006.18. The 2026 single standard deduction under the OBBBA-extended rules is $16,100, which beats $1,037 of itemized deductions. That leaves $6,906.18 of taxable income, taxed entirely at 10%, for $690.62 with no nonrefundable credits. Most models got this wrong in one of four ways: they used a stale or guessed standard deduction ($15,000, $15,350–$15,750), assumed the TCJA sunset ($8,300 plus a $5,300 personal exemption), took the $8,389 ESI premiums out of wages, or worked out about $691 and then submitted a different number.

The only potentially applicable refundable credit is the childless EITC, and its phaseout uses the greater of earned income or adjusted gross income. The $26,006 of wages is earned income; employer-sponsored insurance premiums do not reduce that amount, and at this earnings level the childless EITC is fully phased out. With no qualifying child or student and no applicable rebate or payroll credit, every refundable component is zero.

Louisiana's expansion pathway requires MAGI at or below the applicable adult limit, but the engine computes the head's MAGI income level as 1.44 times FPL, so that pathway fails. The listed employer-sponsored insurance premium is not established as a pre-tax payroll deduction and cannot simply be subtracted from wages; after the applicable MAGI computation, the head qualifies through no Medicaid category.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes are computed from the applicable payroll-tax wage base, and the reference calculation applies the 6.2% and 1.45% employee rates to the full $26,006 of wages. The employer-sponsored insurance premium input does not reduce that wage base in this calculation, producing $1,612.38 of Social Security tax plus $377.09 of Medicare tax, or $1,989.47.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Louisiana’s broad-based categorical eligibility gross-income screen does not itself guarantee a SNAP allotment; the household must still produce an eligible benefit under the net-income and allotment calculations. SNAP countable income does not subtract capital losses, a mortgage balance is not a shelter expense, and a non-elderly, nondisabled household cannot deduct medical expenses. With no listed deductible shelter payment and countable wages of $26,006, this one-person household receives $0.

Louisiana's 2025 reform set a flat 3% rate and a $12,500 single standard deduction, and repealed the personal exemption. Louisiana ended the federal income tax deduction after 2021. Starting in 2026 the standard deduction is indexed for inflation under R.S. 47:294(B). The frozen reference, computed on policyengine-us 2.15.17, uses $12,835: ($23,006.18 AGI − $12,835) × 3% = $305.14. Louisiana first published its 2026 return deduction, $12,838, in RIB 26-019; that gives $305.05, and this output is excluded from scoring under d994. Of the 51 models, 23 answered $315.18 or $315, consistent with the unindexed $12,500 deduction. The others applied pre-reform law (the $4,500 exemption, the 1.85%/3.5% brackets, the federal tax deduction), subtracted ESI premiums or the federal standard deduction, ignored the $3,000 capital-loss cap, or wrongly said Louisiana has no income tax. Developer adjudication (2026-10-06): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_later_law (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 305.14; the value under the published figure is 305.05. The reference rests on a 2026 Louisiana standard deduction of $12,835, which policyengine-us computed from published CPI-U under R.S. 47:294(B) but which no Louisiana publication stated before the 2026-07-03 freeze; Louisiana's first 2026 return amount, $12,838, came in Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019 on 2026-09-28. Excluded under decision d994, which keeps the published-amounts convention for every other reference (reference_audit/2026-10-05-louisiana). Reference depends on law published after the reference freeze; output excluded from scoring (Louisiana Department of Revenue, Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019, dated 2026-09-28: Louisiana's 2026 standard deduction is $12,838 for single and separate filers and $25,676 for the other statuses, the first 2026 return amount Louisiana published).

The models applied Louisiana’s former refundable earned income tax credit, equal to 5% of the federal EITC, to tax year 2026. Louisiana no longer provides that refundable credit in 2026, so the Louisiana refundable-credits computation returns zero regardless of an estimated federal EITC amount.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Under OBBBA, TCJA's rates stay in place for 2026, and the SALT cap is $40,400 for MAGI below $505,000. The frozen reference combines $26,460 in real estate tax with the engine's Maryland withholding estimate, which includes state and county income tax. That total is above the cap, so the SALT deduction is the full $40,400. Itemized deductions are therefore $68,610 ($40,400 SALT plus $28,210 mortgage interest), taxable income is $131,526.91, and the 2026 single brackets (10/12/22/24% with breakpoints at $12,400, $50,400 and $105,700) give $24,164.46. The models fell into four groups: counting only property tax (about $27,510), adding state income tax but not the county tax (about $25,845), using the old $10,000 SALT cap (about $31,400), or assuming TCJA expired (pre-TCJA brackets plus a personal exemption). Developer adjudication (2026-09-29): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 24,164.46; the alternative is 23,772.80. The prompt lists state and local tax refund income without saying whether the refunded tax reduced federal tax in the year it was deducted; policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the whole refund as income (policyengine-us#9422, fixing issue #9122), while under 26 U.S.C. 111(a) none of it is income if the household took no tax benefit from the deduction. Found in the 2026-09-29 engine upgrade (reference_audit/2026-09-28, cluster salt_refund_gross_income_9122). Both models returned 0 without running either test.

Texas imposes no individual state income tax, so a Texas resident has $0 of state income tax before refundable credits regardless of the listed taxable-income deductions or credits. Taxes from other jurisdictions do not apply because the household resides in Texas.

OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent, so 2026 uses a $32,200 MFJ standard deduction and a 10% bracket that ends at $24,800. Gross income is $87,201 and the QBI deduction is $0.20, so taxable income is $55,000.80. The tax is then $2,480 + 12% × $30,200.80 = $6,104.10, and no nonrefundable credits apply. Most models either used pre-OBBBA inflation projections ($30,000–$30,840 standard deduction with a $23,850–$24,500 bracket), assumed the TCJA had expired and used personal exemptions with a 15% bracket, wrongly excluded the ESI premium, or reported a final number that did not match their own math.

With no qualifying children, education expenses, or other credit-triggering facts, and income above the childless EITC range, every refundable component is zero.

Disability alone does not establish North Carolina Medicaid eligibility; the person must qualify through a specific MAGI or traditional categorical pathway and satisfy that pathway's financial rules. The head's household MAGI is $87,201, or 4.03 times FPL, and the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE, so medical expenses, rent, and $1,001 in assets do not create eligibility.

Head is 26, so the age-65 Medicare pathway is closed. Being disabled is not enough for Medicare by itself. Under-65 entitlement requires 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) entitlement, or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or ALS. This household lists no SSDI, and the prompt says unlisted benefits count as zero. All eight models treated the 'is disabled' flag as a direct route to Medicare and answered Yes. The correct answer is No.

The reference applies the 6.2% employee Social Security rate and the 1.45% Medicare rate to each spouse's full listed gross wages: $41,200 and $46,000. That gives 7.65% × $87,200 = $6,670.80. Self-employment tax applies only when net earnings from self-employment reach the filing threshold; the head’s listed $1 produces no liability. There is no minimum $31 self-employment tax or rounding rule that converts this de minimis amount into a positive tax.

PolicyEngine models two of these routes: age 65 or older, or positive SSDI with at least 24 months of SSDI receipt. It does not model the ESRD or ALS pathways. The spouse is 26, receives no SSDI and has no listed months of disability benefit receipt, so the spouse is not Medicare eligible. Every model treated the 'is disabled' flag as enough for Medicare on its own and answered Yes.
