Every model treated age 85 plus disability as enough and either called the income 'low' without testing it against a limit or relied on pathways PolicyEngine does not use: medically needy spend-down, the Wisconsin Medicaid Purchase Plan (MAPP), or Indian Health Service (IHS) coverage.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Only the head's $7,656 of wages is subject to employee FICA. Social Security benefits and survivor benefits are not wages. The correct figure is 6.2% × $7,656 = $474.67 plus 1.45% × $7,656 = $111.01, for $585.68 in total. Wisconsin has no mandatory employee state payroll tax, and Additional Medicare Tax does not apply. Every wrong answer comes from an arithmetic slip, a submitted value that doesn't match the model's own correct calculation, or a missing output. None reflects a different reading of the rules.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Wisconsin FoodShare uses broad-based categorical eligibility through TANF non-cash benefits. Its gross limit is 200% FPL, or $2,608.33 a month for one person, and the household's $2,581.83 falls below it. That makes the household categorically eligible and waives the 100% FPL net income test. Because 30% of the $2,036 net income ($611) exceeds the $298 maximum allotment, this one-person household gets the FY2026 minimum allotment of $24 (8% of $298, rounded to the nearest dollar), or $288 a year. Most models applied the net income test or the "contribution exceeds max = $0" shortcut and missed both the categorical-eligibility pathway and the minimum benefit. Two models found the right pathway but used the older $23 minimum, and a few submitted large benefit amounts that their reasoning did not support.

Every model that gave an answer counted the $10,392 non-SS survivor benefits as taxable, which produced a Wisconsin AGI of $18,048. The $20,590 of annual income in the engine's derivation is wages plus Social Security survivor benefits. The engine treats the $10,392 survivor benefits as nontaxable, so they enter neither federal nor Wisconsin AGI. Social Security is exempt in Wisconsin, so the only taxable income left is $7,656 of wages, and the Wisconsin standard deduction of about $13,000+ brings taxable income to $0. Separately, even on the models' own taxable-income figures, Wisconsin's nonrefundable school property tax credit for renters would have wiped out their liabilities: $7,200 rent becomes $1,440 of rent-equivalent property tax, and 12% of that is a $172.80 credit, more than any model's pre-credit tax of $94 to $162. No model got both points right, so none reached $0.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine leaves the listed $10,392 generic `survivor_benefits` out of both AGI and wi_homestead_income. Wis. Stat. § 71.52(5) adds the gross amount of pensions and annuities, including survivor annuities, to Wisconsin AGI when computing homestead household income. Counting it gives $30,982, which is above the $24,680 limit, so the credit would be $0.
case_annotation: The deciding step is what goes into Wisconsin homestead household income. PolicyEngine's wi_homestead_income counts only wages ($7,656) and Social Security survivor benefits ($12,934), for $20,590, and leaves out the generic $10,392 survivor benefits. That keeps income under the $24,680 limit, and with property tax set at 20% of the $7,200 rent ($1,440) the credit is 0.8 × (1,440 − 0.08785 × (20,590 − 8,060)) = $271.39. Most models added the $10,392 survivor benefits, reached $30,982, and set the credit to zero. The rest either skipped the homestead credit entirely, left out Social Security, or used 25% of rent and the wrong phase-out parameters. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_model_issue_fixed; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 271.39; the alternative is 0.00. The prompt lists survivor benefits other than Social Security without saying what they are. Wisconsin homestead household income counts the gross amount of a survivor pension or annuity (Wis. Stat. 71.52(6); Schedule H line 9d), which is the reading under the alternative value; the reference leaves them out. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (source of survivor_benefits (pension or annuity, or another survivor payment) and taxability of survivor_benefits).

CHIP is limited to children who do not qualify for Medicaid. At approximately $30,000 of household income, the age-9 child qualifies for Florida Medicaid in the OLDER_CHILD category, so Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP eligibility even though the income is below CHIP's upper limit.

Florida's refusal of adult Medicaid expansion does not touch children's coverage: the state's mandatory MAGI pathway for the older-child category (ages 6-18) runs to 133% FPL, and a 9-year-old in a household of five with roughly $21,600 of MAGI sits at 0.72 FPL — barely half the threshold. The only computation required is household MAGI from the $30,000 of self-employment income divided by the family-of-five poverty guideline, then compared with 133% FPL; no asset test, no enrollment fact, and no SSI linkage enters the children's MAGI pathway. Both models returned 0 without ever running that ratio, treating Medicaid eligibility as something the prompt had to assert rather than something the stated income and age determine.

CHIP eligibility requires the child to be ineligible for Medicaid, not merely under age 19 and below CHIP's upper income limit. At age 6 and this household income, child2 qualifies for Medicaid under Florida's OLDER_CHILD category, so the Medicaid–CHIP mutual-exclusivity rule makes child2 ineligible for CHIP.

Head Start eligibility requires satisfying the program’s preschool-age and income rules. Child 2 is age 6, and the household’s approximately $30,000 annual income exceeds the applicable Head Start income threshold in the PolicyEngine calculation; no foster-care or qualifying-assistance exception applies.

The trap is Florida's older-child Medicaid pathway: children ages 6-18 are covered up to 133% FPL, a MAGI category with no asset test and no dependence on the state's refusal to expand adult coverage. With $30,000 of self-employment income for a household of five, MAGI lands at 0.72 x FPL, about half the applicable limit, so child2 qualifies under OLDER_CHILD. All three models conflated Florida's non-expansion posture (which closes only the adult pathway) or a stale 100% FPL children's threshold with the child MAGI test, and each returned 0 on income that clears the real limit with wide margin.

WIC child eligibility ends at the fifth birthday, so a six-year-old cannot qualify through the infant-or-child category regardless of household income. Child 2 is age 6 and has no listed pregnancy or postpartum status, leaving no WIC categorical eligibility pathway.

CHIP eligibility requires the child not already qualify for Medicaid. At age 0 and approximately $30,000 of household income, child3 qualifies for Florida Medicaid under the INFANT category, so the Medicaid eligibility result categorically blocks CHIP eligibility regardless of the higher CHIP income ceiling or the absence of current coverage.

Early Head Start eligibility follows either the income pathway or a categorical pathway; categorical status is not an additional requirement when family income is at or below the applicable poverty threshold. The newborn satisfies the under-age-3 rule, and the five-person household's $30,000 annual income satisfies the benchmark's income test, so the child is eligible.

Head Start for preschool-age children requires both program-specific age eligibility and satisfaction of an eligibility pathway such as the income test. A child age 0 belongs to the Early Head Start age group, not the preschool-age Head Start group, and the household's $30,000 income also exceeds the stated $27,750 threshold.

The dispositive rule is Florida's age-based INFANT Medicaid category, which covers children under age 1 at MAGI up to 185% FPL — a far higher threshold than the adult standards, and one that applies in a non-expansion state. The household's MAGI is 0.72 FPL, so the only two conditions that matter, age under 1 and income under the infant threshold, are both satisfied. All three models denied eligibility by routing the infant through adult or generic standards: one gave no derivation, one required an SSI/disability-style marker that MAGI categories do not use, and one computed the income test correctly and then overrode it with a nonexistent asset test plus a Medicaid-expansion and enrollment requirement.

WIC eligibility is derived from the child's age and household income; it does not require the prompt to explicitly state that the child is WIC-eligible. Child 3 is under age five, and the household's approximately $30,000 annual income is below the 2026 WIC limit of 185% of the federal poverty guideline for a five-person household.

The 2026 married-filing-jointly standard deduction does not reduce this household's taxable income to zero after the deductible half of self-employment tax. The resulting pre-credit income tax is fully offset by $2,792.91 of the $6,600 Child Tax Credit allocated as nonrefundable, and tax after nonrefundable credits is floored at zero rather than becoming negative.

The household's earned income for both credits is $30,000 of self-employment income minus the deductible half of SE tax ($2,119.43), which comes to $27,880.57. That amount sits on the three-child EITC plateau below the 2026 MFJ phase-out start, so the EITC is the full $8,231 maximum. The refundable CTC is 15% × ($27,880.57 − $2,500) = $3,807.09, which is below the 2026 refundable cap of $1,700 × 3 = $5,100 under the CTC as extended in 2025. The wrong answers fall into five groups: models that assumed the TCJA had expired and used a $1,000-per-child ACTC; models that ran the ACTC formula on gross $30,000 or on the 92.35% net SE earnings instead of SE income minus half SE tax; models that applied a nonexistent EITC phase-out; models that misstated the 2026 EITC maximum; and models that denied the credits entirely.

The FREE tier here is over-determined: the household's $8,020.55 SNAP benefit confers categorical free-meal eligibility outright, and independently $30,000 for a five-person household is 78% of the federal poverty guideline, far under the 130% free-meal cutoff. The only fact requiring inference is school attendance — never stated explicitly — which follows from the children aged 9 and 6 being K-12 students, generating $7.15 per child per day net of the $0.87 paid portion for $2,261.92 annually. The trap is the instruction to treat unlisted statuses as false: a model that applies it to school enrollment erases both students and skips both qualifying tests. Both models defaulted to 0 on that reading rather than deriving the students from age and then applying either the SNAP categorical pathway or the 130% FPG income test.

Low MAGI alone does not establish adult Medicaid eligibility in Florida. The age-30 head is not a dependent, receives no SSI, and fits none of Florida's active Medicaid eligibility categories, so the category is NONE despite MAGI income of 0.72 times FPL.

WIC categorical eligibility is individual, not household-wide: only a pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding woman, an infant, or a child under age five can qualify. The infant satisfies that requirement, but the 30-year-old Head has no listed pregnancy, postpartum, or breastfeeding status, so the Head remains ineligible despite the household meeting the income test.

Reduced-price and free school meals are mutually exclusive output tiers in this calculation. The household’s 0.78 school-meal FPG ratio and categorical eligibility place it in the superior FREE tier, so it receives positive free-meal support and no reduced-price support.

The Schedule SE computation here is fully determined: net earnings from self-employment are 92.35% of $30,000 = $27,705, entirely below the Social Security wage base, so the tax is $27,705 × 15.3% = $4,238.865, which PolicyEngine reports as $4,238.86. Every model named the correct base fraction, the correct 15.3% combined rate, and correctly noted the wage base is not binding — none missed a rule. The separation is purely in executing the product: each model reported a whole-dollar figure that is $2 to $6 away from $4,238.87, whereas correct rounding of the true product to whole dollars gives $4,239. The trap is arithmetic precision on 0.9235 × 0.153 × $30,000, not any element of the SE tax rule.

The benefit follows directly from FY2026 parameters: monthly gross income is $2,500. Subtracting the $500 earned income deduction (20%) and the $261 standard deduction for five people leaves $1,739. The $800 rent is below half of that ($869.50), and no utility costs are listed, so there is no excess shelter deduction and no SUA. The expected contribution is 30% of $1,739, rounded up to $522, and $1,183 − $522 = $661 per month, or $7,932 per year. Most models missed by using stale or guessed standard deductions and maximum allotments (FY2025's $1,158 and $254, or the 6+ person $299), by inventing a shelter or utility deduction, or by subtracting SE tax. The closest answers reached $661.30 per month because they skipped the rule that rounds the 30% contribution up to a whole dollar. A few wrongly found the household ineligible or miscounted its size. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (thresholds_rates). The frozen 8,020.55 is regenerated as 7,932.00: it applies the publication rule: SNAP October-December 2026 hold the FY2026 schedule (the SNAP uprating index behind the maximum allotments, deductions, shelter cap and utility allowances), the last USDA published before the 2026-07-03 reference freeze; USDA published FY2027 on 2026-08-21. The poverty guideline is the 2026 HHS guideline, published in January 2026. The engine's SNAP rounding defects are root causes r26, r27, r28 and r31, fixed upstream and applied with the convention.; it corrects an engine defect fixed upstream (fixed in PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#9318 (merged 2026-08-25), after the reference freeze): If 30% of net income ends in cents, the state rounds it up to the next dollar or rounds the allotment down to the next dollar; with a whole-dollar maximum allotment both give the same whole-dollar allotment. Reference regenerated (7 U.S.C. 2012(u), 2017(a); USDA FY2026 SNAP COLA memorandum (signed 2025-08-14); 7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(A)).

Florida’s non-expansion Medicaid program does not provide a general low-income pathway for a nondisabled 29-year-old adult. The spouse qualifies through no categorical pathway: household MAGI exceeds Florida’s parent/caretaker limit, and the presence of an infant does not establish pregnancy or postpartum status.

WIC eligibility for an adult requires the adult herself to be pregnant, breastfeeding, or within the applicable postpartum period; merely living with an infant does not establish any of those statuses. The prompt makes every unlisted status false, so the spouse is not pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding and fails categorical eligibility regardless of household income.

The 2026 rules are permanent TCJA as extended by OBBBA. That means a $16,100 single standard deduction and brackets of 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 and 24% above that. The traditional IRA deduction is phased out for an active plan participant with AGI near $170k. ESI premiums are not taken out of the $95,755 of wages. No overtime income is listed, so there is no overtime deduction. Most often missed: the new non-itemizer cash charitable deduction ($387, up to $1,000 for a single filer). It cuts taxable income to $153,455, so ordinary tax is $19,615 on $112,572 and the 15% tax on $40,884 of qualified dividends and long-term gains is $6,133, for $25,748. Many models stopped at $25,841 because they left out the $387 deduction. Others brought back pre-TCJA personal exemptions and miscellaneous itemized deductions, subtracted ESI premiums from wages, or made up an overtime deduction.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The reference applies employee FICA to the full $100,000 of stated gross wages: 6.2% Social Security ($6,200, well under the wage base) plus 1.45% Medicare ($1,450). That totals $7,650, and there is no Additional Medicare Tax because wages are below $200,000. The household facts never say the $6,889 employer-sponsored insurance premium is a Section 125 salary reduction, and the prompt says not to infer unlisted facts. The largest group of models still subtracted it from FICA wages and reported $7,123. The other wrong answers came from excluding the 401(k) deferral from FICA wages, applying Additional Medicare Tax to non-wage income, or submitting a value that did not match the model's own reasoning.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Ohio AGI equals federal AGI of $169,942.94: wages net of the $4,245 traditional 401(k), plus interest, dividends, capital gains and estate income. There is no IRA deduction, no Ohio addback, and no itemized or standard deduction. Subtracting the $1,900 personal exemption for income over $80,000 leaves $168,042.94 of taxable income. Under the 2026 Ohio schedule, the tax is a fixed $332 base plus 2.75% of the amount over $26,050, which gives $4,236.81, and no nonrefundable credits apply. The most common mistakes were dropping the $332 base (which gives $3,905), using the repealed 3.5%/3.125% bracket above $100,000 or the old $360.69 base, and misstating AGI, mostly by subtracting the $6,889 of employer health premiums or the phased-out $198 IRA contribution.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The IRA distribution produces $18,240 of adjusted gross income, while the Social Security retirement benefit is not taxable under the joint-return provisional-income thresholds. The applicable standard deduction eliminates taxable income, so the tax computation yields $0; both models expressly derived zero taxable income and zero liability but then submitted unsupported positive amounts.

At 72, the head is outside the ACA expansion-adult category, which covers ages 19–64 up to 138% FPL. Their MAGI is also about 202% FPL, so that pathway fails twice. The head gets no SSI, so the SSI-recipient route is closed. The aged/blind/disabled route has an income limit near the SSI/100% FPL level, roughly $1,000–$1,300 a month. The head's unearned income is about $3,637 a month, so it is far over that limit even after the $20 general disregard. All four models treated being aged, blind or disabled plus low assets as enough to qualify and skipped the income test, which leaves medicaid_category = NONE.

Employee payroll taxes apply to covered wages and other employment compensation, not Social Security retirement benefits or taxable IRA distributions. Because neither spouse has wages or other employee compensation, the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory Washington employee payroll-tax bases are all zero, yielding $0.

Washington's 200% gross-income screening rule does not itself establish categorical SNAP eligibility or guarantee the minimum allotment. This two-person household's approximately $43,640 annual income disqualifies it, so the minimum-benefit rule never applies and annual SNAP equals $0.

The spouse is 49, so the only adult MAGI route is Washington's expansion group, which has a limit of 138% FPL. Medicaid MAGI adds back nontaxable Social Security, so tax-unit MAGI is $25,400 + $18,240 = $43,640, or 2.02x FPL, which is above the limit. Being blind or disabled does not open a separate pathway with no income limit. PolicyEngine's disability-based route depends on SSI receipt, and the couple's combined countable income of about $43,640 is far above the SSI couple benefit rate, so SSI = 0 and medicaid_category = NONE. Most models assumed disability alone qualified the spouse, or treated the spouse as having $0 countable income. The rest left Social Security out of MAGI.

Under age 65, a person qualifies for Medicare through disability only after 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits (42 U.S.C. 426(b)), or through the ESRD or ALS pathways. PolicyEngine models the same rule: the age-65 test or at least 24 months of Social Security disability receipt. The spouse is 49 and flagged disabled, but the household lists no Social Security disability income, no months of SSDI receipt, and no ESRD or ALS, so the spouse fails every pathway. All ten models treated the disability flag alone as enough for Medicare. They skipped the separate requirement of 24 months of SSDI entitlement.

The trap is the $13,000 "financial assistance" line: in PolicyEngine `financial_assistance` is a non-taxable cash receipt (counted for benefit means-tests, never in gross income or AGI), so the only taxable items here are $5,923 of wages and $1,920 of farm rent income, reduced by the $3,000 capital-loss limitation on the -$9,944 long-term loss, for AGI of roughly $4,843. That sits far below the 2026 single standard deduction (~$16,100), leaving taxable income of $0, no NIIT (net investment income is a $3,000 loss), and no add-on liabilities, hence $0. Both models handled the $3,000 capital-loss cap and the standard deduction correctly but pushed the $13,000 gift/assistance through as ordinary income, manufacturing $1,743 of taxable income and a $174.30 bracket tax. Excluding the non-taxable transfer collapses the entire computation to zero.

The only refundable credit is the childless EITC. The head is 31, so they meet the age 25–64 rule, and the credit phases in at 7.65% of earned income: 7.65% × $5,923 in gross wages = $453.10. AGI is $4,843: $5,923 in wages plus $1,920 in farm rent, minus the capital loss capped at $3,000, with the $13,000 of financial assistance excluded. That AGI is far below the phase-out threshold, and farm rent of $1,920 is far below the investment-income limit, so neither one reduces the credit. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they denied that a worker without children gets an EITC, they used the ESI premiums to wipe out earned income, or they mixed AGI into the phase-in step, which uses earned income only.

Texas does not provide MAGI Medicaid eligibility to a nondependent, childless 31-year-old merely because income is below an income threshold. The head meets the immigration requirement but belongs to none of Texas's active Medicaid categories, so the low 0.30-FPL MAGI level does not create eligibility.

WIC requires both financial eligibility and membership in a qualifying demographic category: pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding women, infants, or children under age five. The 31-year-old head has no listed qualifying status, and unlisted statuses are false, so passing the income test does not establish WIC eligibility.

Employer-sponsored insurance premiums are not automatically employee pre-tax cafeteria-plan deductions from FICA wages; the listed $5,923 remains subject to employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. PolicyEngine computes $367.22 of Social Security tax and $85.88 of Medicare tax, totaling $453.10, with no Additional Medicare Tax or mandatory Texas employee payroll tax.

Self-employment tax applies only to positive net earnings from self-employment, after determining the applicable self-employment tax base. The household’s relevant net income is approximately -$2,101, so there are no positive net self-employment earnings and the tax base is zero; treating the $1,920 farm rent entry as a standalone positive self-employment tax base produces the wrong liability.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's SNAP unearned-income source list leaves out farm_rent_income, so the $1,920 of passive farm rent never enters SNAP gross income. 7 CFR 273.9(b)(2)(ii) counts rental-property income as unearned income when the member does not actively manage the property 20+ hours a week, and counting it raises net income to about $1,429/month, above the 100% FPL net limit of $1,304.17, which makes SNAP $0.
case_annotation: The $287.68 annual reference is frozen and excluded from scoring because weekly work hours were unlisted. The 2.60.0 recheck returns $0 under its default reading, which does not settle the ambiguity. The current engine counts farm rent as SNAP unearned income, and Texas BBCE does not apply the net income test to this household. For an eligible one-person household, the held FY2026 schedule gives a rounded $24 monthly minimum allotment. Most models counted the farm rent, which put net income near $1,430, above 100% FPL, so they found the household ineligible. Others either dropped the $13,000 of financial assistance and got large benefits, or treated '30% of net income exceeds the maximum' as $0 and skipped the minimum allotment. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (categorical_eligibility). The frozen reference is 287.68; the alternative is 0.00. The prompt lists no hours worked and says to treat unlisted numeric inputs as 0; the reference assumed 40 hours a week, which clears the SNAP work requirement for able-bodied adults without dependents. Under the zero-hours reading the time limit applies, which ends benefits after three countable months unless an exemption or area waiver applies; the alternative value is the engine's zero-hours result, not a certified entitlement. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (weekly_hours_worked_before_lsr).

Most models got AGI right ($106,573). Some applied pre-TCJA "sunset" law or omitted the OBBBA senior deduction; others used different readings of unlisted withholding and Medicare inputs. The frozen reference uses the 2026 OBBBA rules: the 10%/12%/22% brackets with breakpoints at $12,400 and $50,400, and the $6,000 senior deduction phased down by 6% of MAGI above $75,000, leaving $4,105.65. It adds a 20% QBI deduction of $4,872.35 and itemized deductions of $24,787.23. The itemized total includes an unlisted $5,367.30 Virginia withholding estimate and an imputed $2,434.80 Medicare Part B premium. It excludes OTC costs and applies the 0.5%-of-AGI charity floor, leaving the reference's taxable income at $72,807.33 and tax at $10,729.61. Recorded alternatives are $11,969.80 without withholding, the local sales-tax estimate or a Part B premium, and $11,642.16 using Virginia liability without a Part B premium; several models match these alternatives. This output remains excluded from scoring for dependence on unlisted inputs. Developer adjudication (2026-10-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 10,729.61; the alternative is 11,137.31. The prompt lists no state income tax withheld or paid during 2026; policyengine-us 2.15.17 fills the state income tax part of the federal state and local tax deduction with state_withheld_income_tax, a formula estimate of Virginia withholding on federal AGI ($5,367.30), while read as the household paying its 2026 Virginia income tax during the year the deduction takes the engine's liability ($3,514.15). The reference's medical deduction also counts a modeled Medicare Part B premium ($2,434.80) the prompt does not list; without it the output is 11,265.27. Found in the 2026-10-05 audits of the state income tax in SALT (reference_audit/2026-10-05) and of the Part B premium (reference_audit/2026-10-05-medicare-part-b). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (state income tax withheld or paid during 2026, which the federal state and local tax deduction takes as its state income tax part; policyengine-us fills it with state_withheld_income_tax, a formula estimate on federal AGI that the household data never set; also Medicare enrollment and a Medicare Part B premium paid during 2026, which the medical expense deductions count; policyengine-us treats every Medicare-eligible person as enrolled (takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true, so medicare_enrolled follows is_medicare_eligible) and adds the modeled premium (medicare_part_b_premium) to medical expenses, and the household data never set either).

EITC phaseout uses adjusted gross income or earned income, whichever is greater, rather than wages alone. This filer’s partnership/S-corp income, taxable retirement distributions, pension, taxable Social Security, and interest raise AGI far above the childless EITC limit, so every refundable credit component is zero.

The requested payroll-tax output includes employee Social Security and employee Medicare taxes on the $22,700 of wages, while self-employment tax is reported separately and Virginia adds no mandatory employee payroll tax here. The stated components sum to $1,407.40 + $329.15 = $1,736.55; arbitrary adjustments, duplication, and invented state payroll taxes produce the wrong answers.

The household's only business-type input is $24,362 of partnership or S-corp income, and that amount is not net earnings from self-employment. S-corp pass-through income is never subject to SE tax. A partnership distributive share counts only for a general partner, and the prompt says any unlisted status is false, so no general-partner status can be assumed. With zero self-employment income, SE tax is $0. Every substantive wrong answer made the same mistake: each model counted the partnership/S-corp amount as SE earnings, then applied 15.3% to 92.35% of it, which gives about $3,442. Some models then added further arithmetic errors on top of that.

Virginia AGI is $86,743.77, which is federal AGI minus the $19,828.80 of taxable Social Security. The single filer's $50,000 AFAGI threshold eliminates the $12,000 age deduction entirely. When the engine counts neither its unlisted Part B premium as a medical expense nor its $5,367.30 Virginia withholding estimate in federal SALT, it takes the standard deduction. As computed, the filer itemizes federally in the engine, so Virginia itemized deductions apply. Those are $19,419.94 in total. Charitable gifts are $10,913.78 after the 2026 0.5%-of-AGI floor. Medical is $4,441.86, which counts the $2,434.80 Medicare Part B premium but not the $2,000 of OTC expenses. Real estate tax is $4,064. Exemptions are $1,730 ($930 personal plus $800 aged), giving taxable income of $65,593.83 and tax of $3,514.15. The model answers include four recurring paths: taking a Virginia standard deduction, keeping an age deduction that is phased out, dropping the $800 aged exemption, or building itemized deductions as $17,518. That $17,518 figure omits the Part B premium and skips the charitable floor. Developer adjudication (2026-10-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 3,514.15; the alternative is 3,654.15. The prompt lists no Medicare enrollment or Part B premium; policyengine-us 2.15.17 treats the 69-year-old head as enrolled (takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true) and adds the $2,434.80 standard Part B premium to medical expenses, which Virginia's itemized deductions carry from the federal ones; read with no premium paid, the output is the alternative. Found in the 2026-10-05 audit of the Part B premium (reference_audit/2026-10-05-medicare-part-b, scripts/sweep_part_b.py). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (Medicare enrollment and a Medicare Part B premium paid during 2026, which the medical expense deductions count; policyengine-us treats every Medicare-eligible person as enrolled (takes_up_medicare_if_eligible defaults to true, so medicare_enrolled follows is_medicare_eligible) and adds the modeled premium (medicare_part_b_premium) to medical expenses, and the household data never set either).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Age 77 and a reported disability do not by themselves place the head in an Alabama Medicaid eligibility category. PolicyEngine assigns medicaid_category = NONE; the 1.47 FPL MAGI amount therefore cannot establish eligibility through a MAGI category, and immigration eligibility alone is insufficient.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

SNAP eligibility uses approximately $23,442 of annual household income here: $18,708 of Social Security plus $4,734 of tax-exempt interest. That income exceeds PolicyEngine’s applicable one-person SNAP eligibility limit, so the calculation stops at ineligibility and returns $0; deductions and minimum-allotment rules do not create a benefit for an ineligible household.

Alabama exempts Social Security, but it does not follow the federal exclusion for municipal-bond interest. Alabama gross income includes interest on obligations of other states. Alabama allows a single filer only a $3,000 standard deduction at this AGI plus a $1,500 personal exemption, with no extra deduction for age or disability. That leaves $234 of taxable income, taxed at 2% for $4.68. Every model answered $0. Most treated federally tax-exempt interest as also exempt in Alabama. Several models considered adding it back but overstated the deductions as large enough to wipe out $4,734.

SNAP’s minimum allotment applies only after a household passes the program’s eligibility tests; it cannot override failure of the gross-income test. At $52,800 of annual household income, this household exceeds the applicable 2026 gross-income limit, so the computation stops with no SNAP benefit.

Florida did not expand Medicaid, so a childless, non-pregnant 42-year-old has no MAGI adult or parent category, even with MAGI at 0% FPL (veterans benefits are left out of MAGI). Disability alone does not create eligibility. The disabled pathway requires either receiving SSI or passing Florida's aged/disabled income test. The spouse's $52,800 in veterans benefits counts as unearned income under SSI-related rules, which pushes SSI to $0 and puts the spouse far above the aged/disabled income limit, so medicaid_category is NONE. All three models treated disability status as enough to qualify and never applied the income test that comes with the disabled pathway.

Under age 65, Medicare eligibility comes only from 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance (Title II) entitlement or from ESRD/ALS. A disability flag on its own does not confer it. The spouse is 42 and receives $52,800 in veterans benefits, which are VA payments and not SSDI. With SSDI income and SSDI months both unlisted, they are 0 under the prompt's rules, so the age test and the SSDI-duration test both fail. All four models treated "is disabled" (plus, for one model, VA benefits) as enough for disability-based Medicare, and so answered Yes.

Early Head Start eligibility requires both an age-qualified child and satisfaction of the program's low-income eligibility rules; being under age 3 is not independently sufficient. Although Child 3 meets the age condition, household income of approximately $250,733 is far above the applicable poverty-based income limit, so the income test produces no eligibility.

Age alone does not establish Head Start eligibility; the child must also qualify through an applicable eligibility pathway, principally the program's low-income criteria in this case. This household's approximately $250,733 income exceeds the relevant poverty-based threshold, so Child 3 is not eligible.

WIC child eligibility requires both categorical eligibility and financial eligibility; being age 2 satisfies only the child-category requirement. The household's approximately $250,733 annual income exceeds the WIC limit of 185% of the federal poverty guideline for a five-person household, so Child 3 is not eligible.

This case tests 2026 law after OBBBA. AGI is $250,733.36: wages, plus the $2,589 refund, minus the $530 loss. From that, three deductions apply: the $32,200 joint standard deduction, the full $25,000 qualified overtime deduction, and the $2,000 charitable deduction for non-itemizers. The overtime deduction is not reduced because the joint phase-out starts at $300,000 MAGI. Itemizing does not beat this $34,200 combination. Taxable income is $191,533.36. The permanent TCJA brackets (10% to $24,800, 12% to $100,800, then 22%) give $31,561.34 of tax. The only nonrefundable credit is the $6,600 CTC ($2,200 × 3 children under 17). The CDCC is $0 because Head has no earned income, and mortgage interest is $0 because only a loan balance is given. Most wrong answers left out the overtime deduction or reduced it, applied TCJA-sunset rules, made up mortgage interest, claimed a CDCC, or skipped the $2,000 charitable deduction. The prompt lists state and local tax refund income without saying whether the refunded tax reduced federal tax in the year it was deducted; policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the whole refund as income (policyengine-us#9422, fixing issue #9122), while under 26 U.S.C. 111(a) none of it is income if the household took no tax benefit from the deduction. The refundable CTC (ACTC) is capped at the part of the child tax credit left over after the credit has offset income tax. This couple files jointly with about $250,733 of AGI. That is below the $400,000 CTC phase-out, so the full $2,200-per-child CTC ($6,600) is allowed. Their federal income tax is well over $25,000, which absorbs the whole $6,600 as a nonrefundable credit and leaves nothing to refund. EITC is zero at this income, and no other refundable credit applies, so the total is $0. The wrong answers skipped the tax-liability limit and treated the per-child refundable cap ($1,700 or $1,800), or a made-up fraction of it, as money the family receives automatically.

On income alone, the household is in the paid tier. Its $248,675 in wages is 6.43 times the 5-person poverty guideline, and it has no SNAP or TANF categorical eligibility. Arkansas Act 123 of 2025 (A.C.A. § 6-18-722(f)) separately gives every public school student one free breakfast a day starting in the 2025-26 school year, whatever the family income. PolicyEngine assumes the two K-12 children (ages 16 and 11) take it, which is worth $2.06 per child per day over 180 days, or $741.60 a year. Because free school meal support is positive, the answer is Yes. Every model ruled out free school meal support and missed this Arkansas universal-breakfast rule.

The `ssi` output is the federal SSI payment only. Take the 2026 federal benefit rate of $994/month and subtract countable unearned income of $213.33/month ($2,800/12 = $233.33 in Social Security, minus the $20/month general exclusion). The wrong answers fall into four groups: adding a NY living-alone supplement of about $87/month ($1,044/year) on top, using a stale or wrongly projected benefit rate ($943, $967, $990, $991, $982.67), taking the $20 exclusion once a year instead of every month, or calling the person ineligible by comparing $2,800 of annual income against a monthly benefit rate.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine uses NY AGI as household gross income for the real property tax credit, so the $2,800 of nontaxable Social Security is left out. NY Tax Law §606(e) and Form IT-214 (line 10) count that Social Security in household gross income. Counting it puts the household in the $2,001–$3,000 band, where the age-65+ maximum is $341, not the $375 maximum for $1,000 or less.
case_annotation: The key step is recognizing New York's real property tax credit (Tax Law §606(e), IT-214) as a refundable credit for low-income homeowners. It needs no tax liability, earned income, children or rent. This 74-year-old homeowner has federal AGI of $0 and property taxes of $1,634, above 3.5% of that AGI, so the flat table in force from 2025 gives $375. Most models checked only for the EITC and child credits and returned $0. Other models used the repealed household-gross-income rule, applied an incorrect credit formula or amount, or added the nonrefundable household credit. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). From 2025 New York keys the real property tax credit to federal AGI and a flat table; with federal AGI of $0 and property tax above 3.5% of it, a filer 65 or older receives $375. The judge applied the repealed household-gross-income rule. Reference affirmed (N.Y. Tax Law 606(e) as amended by Part RR of Chapter 59 of the Laws of 2025).

Under 2026 law as amended by OBBBA, the TCJA structure is permanent. That means a $24,150 head-of-household standard deduction, 10%/12% brackets, a $2,200 CTC per child under 17, and a CDCC rate of 35% at this AGI. Applied to $28,418.54 of taxable income, this gives $3,056.23 of tax before credits. That tax is fully absorbed in order by the CDCC ($546), the Saver's Credit ($200, which is 10% of the $2,000 contribution cap), and $2,310.23 of the $4,400 CTC. The CTC alone already exceeds the pre-credit tax. Most models either assumed the TCJA expired and used a $1,000-per-child CTC, used single filing status, or wrongly limited the nonrefundable CTC to the amount left over after the ACTC refundable cap. The nonrefundable CTC is applied against tax liability first, and only the unused part becomes refundable.

Every wrong model pushed the ratio under 1.85 one of three ways: netting pre-tax and premium amounts out of the income base ($46,180), counting a fourth household member, or asserting the 130–185% band without ever dividing income by the guideline. The trap is that the household's income sits just 19 points above the cutoff, so any one of those shortcuts flips the answer.

To get Virginia taxable income of $39,468.54 and tax of $2,011.94, you start from federal AGI of $52,568.54 and take three subtractions: the 2026 standard deduction of $8,750, three $930 exemptions ($2,790), and the $1,560 child and dependent care expense deduction. Virginia then allows a nonrefundable EITC equal to 20% of the federal EITC ($1,276.30 → $255.26), which brings the result to $1,756.68. Most models missed one or more of these steps. They left out the nonrefundable VA EITC, skipped the $1,560 care deduction or swapped it for a nonexistent VA care credit, used an old $8,000/$8,500 standard deduction, or cut AGI a second time by subtracting ESI premiums already excluded from wages.

Virginia's earned income credit is an either/or election. A filer takes the nonrefundable credit (20% of federal EITC) or the refundable credit, never both, and PolicyEngine counts the refundable version only when it beats the nonrefundable credit the filer can actually use. This head of household earns about $55,000, so Virginia tax liability is roughly $2,000 or more. That fully absorbs a nonrefundable credit worth a few hundred dollars, so the household takes the nonrefundable credit and va_refundable_credits is $0. Every model that answered added a refundable Virginia EITC on top of the regular credit, treating it as automatic and stackable instead of as the alternative to the nonrefundable credit.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Two facts drive the $0: PolicyEngine's `disability_benefits` input is a non-taxable income source excluded from AGI, so AGI is wages only ($25,665), and the household's medical costs ($2,200 non-Medicare-Part-B premiums + $30,000 other medical + $400 over-the-counter = $32,600) generate an itemized medical expense deduction of $32,600 − 7.5% × $25,665 ($1,925) = $30,675. That itemized total exceeds AGI, so taxable income floors at $0 and there is no tax to reduce with nonrefundable credits. Every wrong model either taxed the disability benefits, ignored the medical itemized deduction, or both, leaving a positive 10%/12%-bracket residue. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 0.00; the alternative is 875.34. The prompt lists disability benefits from employment without saying who paid for the coverage. Benefits from employer-paid coverage are included in gross income (26 U.S.C. 105(a)); benefits from coverage the employee paid for with after-tax money are excluded (26 U.S.C. 104(a)(3)). The reference excludes them; the alternative value includes them. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (who paid for the coverage behind listed employment disability benefits, which decides whether they are taxable).

The childless EITC phaseout must use the greater of earned income or adjusted gross income. The $13,044 of disability benefits raises AGI above the 2026 childless EITC income limit, so the EITC and total federal refundable credits are $0; all three models instead treated $17,276 of net wages as both earned income and AGI.

The trap is that the `is_disabled` flag by itself opens no Medicaid category in South Carolina. The non-MAGI disability route runs through SSI receipt, and SSI here is $0 because $25,665 in wages plus $13,044 of disability benefits leave countable income far above the SSI federal benefit rate (~$12,000/year) after the $20 general and $65-plus-half earned disregards. The MAGI route fails too: MAGI counts only the taxable wages ($25,665 = 1.61 x FPL for a one-person unit, since child support and the disability benefits are excluded), which sits above SC's parent/caretaker limit, above the 138% FPL expansion limit SC has not adopted, and is moot anyway because no child is present to establish a parent/caretaker category. Every wrong model substituted a program the engine does not implement and that this income fails regardless — a working-disabled buy-in at 250% FPL, a medically needy spend-down against the $30,000 of medical expenses, or a bare disability presumption — instead of testing an actual pathway, so medicaid_category is NONE and eligibility is False.

PolicyEngine grants Medicare eligibility under 65 only through Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) receipt lasting at least 24 months (months_receiving_social_security_disability ≥ 24) or through end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The listed "disability benefits" amount is a generic disability-income input, not Social Security disability. No months of SSDI receipt were given, so under the prompt's rules that count is 0, and being flagged "is disabled" does not by itself make someone Medicare-eligible. The head is 53, has no qualifying SSDI duration and no ESRD, so they are not eligible. Every model treated the disabled flag plus generic disability income as SSDI and assumed the 24-month waiting period was already met, even though the prompt forbids inferring unlisted benefit receipt.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The listed employer-sponsored insurance premium is not specified as a pre-tax payroll deduction, so it does not reduce FICA wages under the prompt’s rule that unlisted statuses are false. Applying 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare to the full $25,665 of wages yields $1,591.23 and $372.14, totaling $1,963.37.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The question is whether this household counts as an elderly/disabled SNAP household. PolicyEngine follows the USDA definition, which requires receipt of a qualifying disability program such as SSI or SSDI. A generic `is_disabled` flag plus generic "disability benefits" income does not meet it. So the gross income test applies, and the head's $39,909 gross income ($3,326/month from wages, disability benefits and child support) fails it. The household's gross income also exceeds SC's broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE) ceiling of 130% of the applicable poverty guideline, so SNAP is $0. Every substantive model treated the head as SNAP-disabled and skipped the gross test. Most also took the uncapped excess medical deduction, which is only available to elderly/disabled households, and so reached roughly the maximum allotment.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

South Carolina's tax base starts from federal taxable income, and this filer's deductible medical outlays total $32,600 ($30,000 other medical expenses + $2,200 health insurance premiums excluding Medicare Part B + $400 over-the-counter health expenses). Netted against the 7.5%-of-AGI floor (at most $2,903 on the largest possible AGI of $38,709), that leaves roughly $30,000 of itemized medical deduction — nearly double the $16,100 single standard deduction — which wipes out federal taxable income, and SC's subtraction for the disabled filer's disability income removes anything left, so SC taxable income never reaches the top of the zero-rate bracket and the tax is $0. Every wrong model defaulted to the standard deduction and treated the $30,000 medical line as an irrelevant household fact; several compounded that with invented SC rate schedules and a nonexistent personal exemption. The gap between $0 and every submitted number is entirely the unclaimed itemized medical expense deduction — no bracket or rate correction closes it. AGI is $70,646, which includes 85% of Social Security ($27,200). Taxable income is $43,446.18. The $1,824 of qualified dividends is taxed at 0%, and the remaining $41,622.18 is taxed at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% after that, for a total of $4,746.66. The wrong answers fall into four groups: models that left out the $1,000 charitable deduction (about $120 too high), models that left out the $6,000 senior deduction, models that used the old TCJA-expiration rules (personal exemption, 15% bracket, miscellaneous itemized deductions), and models that made unsupported jumps to $0 or to unrelated figures.

Minnesota tax starts from federal AGI of $70,646. It then subtracts the full $27,200 of federally taxable Social Security, because AGI is well below the phase-out threshold. Next comes the 2026 standard deduction of $19,300, which includes two aged/blind add-ons and exceeds the available itemized deductions. Finally, the non-itemizer charitable subtraction is $4,977, which is 50% of contributions over $500 after the 2026 0.5%-of-AGI floor. That leaves $19,169 taxed entirely at 5.35%, or $1,025.54. Minnesota's pension subtraction applies only to public pension income, so it does not reach this filer's private pension or IRA income, no personal exemption for the filer, and no elderly subtraction at this income. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they skipped or only partly applied the Social Security subtraction (answers near $2,400–$3,200), left out the non-itemizer charitable subtraction (answers near $1,250–$1,400), or invented exclusions or credits that brought the tax to $0.

Every model that answered 'Yes' skipped the income ceiling: either it assumed PA's full-cost CHIP makes any income eligible, or it looked only at the child's age.

The Child Tax Credit is a nonrefundable credit first; the additional child tax credit is only the residual the taxpayer cannot use against liability, further capped at $1,700 per child in 2026 and at 15% of earnings above $2,500. This household's $145,002 of income less the 2026 MFJ standard deduction leaves roughly $112,800 of taxable income and about $14,000 of federal income tax before refundable credits, which absorbs the entire CTC for the 16-year-old, and the one-child EITC is long gone at joint income above $57,000 — so total federal refundable credits are $0. Every wrong model stopped at the earned-income phase-in and the $400,000 MAGI phase-out and paid out a per-child refundable cap ($1,500, $1,600, $1,700, $2,000, or $2,400) as if the ACTC were a standalone entitlement. One model additionally fabricated a $205 EITC at an income level far past its phase-out.

Income of $145,002 is 5.31 times the $27,320 FPG for three, so both meals land in the federal PAID tier and the 130%/185% income tests never qualify this household. It makes breakfast free for the 16-year-old K-12 student at any income, worth $2.06/day ($2.90 subsidy minus $0.84 paid rate) × 180 days = $370.80. Positive free-meal support yields 1. Every model that answered stopped at the federal NSLP income test and never applied the state's universal breakfast.
